title: Приглашение на семейный обед  (Invitation to a Family Dinner)

segments.t: At the table, Nastya's mother brings up the awkward fact that Kostya punched her husband during their previous misunderstanding, prompting Nastya to make Kostya apologize on the spot. To end the family feud, Nastya invites her parents to visit their apartment for a vegetarian dinner.
Что вы избили моего мужа.
Мама, во-первых, Костя не виноват.
А во-вторых, ему все равно стыдно.
Скажи, Костя.
Скажи, что тебе стыдно.
Мне стыдно.
Настя, я пойду?
Приезжай в субботу к нам домой.
И закончим этот глупый конфликт.
Так приезжайте вы к нам с Костей.
Настя, дорогая, ты поезжай, а я потом как-нибудь.
Значит так.
Боюсь, что папе это будет очень сложно объяснить.
Let's replay the exchange and look closely at each Russian phrase.
Что вы избили моего мужа.
'That you beat up my husband.' The meaning hinges on 'what' working together with 'husband' in spoken Russian.
Мама, во-первых, Костя не виноват.
'Mom, first of all, it was not Kostya's fault.' The grammar packs 'mum' and 'guilty' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange. Kostya answers right away.
А во-вторых, ему все равно стыдно.
'And secondly, he feels ashamed about it anyway.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'and' and finishing on 'ashamed'.
Скажи, Костя.
'Tell her, Kostya.' Nastya brings out the contrast between 'say' and 'Kostya' in a few short words.
Скажи, что тебе стыдно.
'Tell her that you are ashamed.' Notice how Russian expresses 'say' and 'ashamed' with crisp inflection rather than helper words. Nastya answers right away.
Мне стыдно.
'I am ashamed.' Notice how Russian expresses 'for me' and 'ashamed' with crisp inflection rather than helper words.
Настя, я пойду?
'Nastya, may I go back to work now?' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'Nastya' before landing on 'go'.
Приезжай в субботу к нам домой.
'Come visit us at our house on Saturday.' In Russian, the idea of 'come over' flows naturally into 'home' without extra filler words. Kostya answers right away.
И закончим этот глупый конфликт.
'And let us put an end to this foolish conflict.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'both' before landing on 'conflict'.
Так приезжайте вы к нам с Костей.
'Why do the two of you not come visit Kostya and me instead.' Nastya anchors the line on 'like this', while 'Kostya' completes the thought.
Настя, дорогая, ты поезжай, а я потом как-нибудь.
'Nastya, darling, you come visit us, and I will drop by another time.' Kostya addresses the listener with the informal singular 'you' alongside 'somehow'. Nastya answers right away.
Значит так.
'Here is how it is going to be.' Nastya brings out the contrast between 'so' and 'like this' in a few short words.
Боюсь, что папе это будет очень сложно объяснить.
'I am afraid that will be very hard to explain to Dad.' Kostya brings out the contrast between 'am afraid' and 'what' in a few short words. Let's hear the complete conversation once more.

That wraps up this scene as nastya's mother reminds Kostya how he accidentally punched Nastya's father during their last encounter and invites them over on Saturday to make peace—until Nastya invites her parents to their apartment instead. Until next time!
До встречи!
